policy_title: Introduce a Rights of Nature Act
stated: Pass a new Rights of Nature Act to grant nature legal personhood, set soil quality standards, immediately phase out harmful pesticides like glyphosate, and introduce rigorous tests for all pesticides.

source.quote: Greens in parliament will make it a priority to pass a new Rights of Nature Act. For the first time, it would give Nature legal personhood, meaning that it could not be exploited for financial gain. The Act would also set standards for soil quality and phasing out the most harmful pesticides immediately (including glyphosate) and, as we move towards regenerative farming methods, introduce rigorous tests for all pesticides. Only pesticides that pass this test, and demonstrably don’t harm bees, butterflies and other wildlife, would be approved for use in UK and we would end the emergency authorisation of bee-killing pesticides.

bearing_set.reason: Granting nature legal personhood, setting soil quality standards, and phasing out glyphosate/other pesticides directly and substantially affect environmental quality — soil health, water contamination from run-off, and biodiversity — earning a real verdict here.

Glyphosate is one of the most widely-used herbicides in UK agriculture; a rapid phase-out would plausibly raise crop production costs and feed through to food prices, a core cost-of-living essential, warranting a non-negligible verdict on affordability.

membership_note: O6 is the primary and designed-for outcome; O2 captures the concrete agricultural-cost-to-food-price tradeoff from the glyphosate phase-out. O13 (aggregate prosperity) is tempted but UK agriculture is under 1% of GDP so the aggregate productivity effect likely does not clear the non-negligible bar — the food-price channel (O2) is more direct and material. O10 (property rights/coercion) was considered given new land-use mandates but routine environmental regulation does not reach non-negligible on that indicator.
